title: The Open Lodging
question: Rumi compares the mind to a lodging where joy, grief, and shame arrive as unexpected visitors. What building should the self become?
correctExplanation: A guest house — every feeling welcomed, entertained, and released. Hospitality toward emotions instead of eviction.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is guest house. Rumi's lodging receives each visitor courteously, even the dark ones, because each was sent as a guide. Welcome replaces resistance.
lessonContent:
Feelings arrive as visitors, not residents.
Hospitality beats eviction for every emotion.
Dark arrivals often carry guidance in disguise.
Meet, entertain, and release — then sweep the house.
Share this: welcome one unwelcome feeling as a guest tonight.

title: The Lit Wound
question: Rumi's most quoted paradox claims the injury itself is the opening. Through what does the light enter?
correctExplanation: The wound — breakage as aperture. What hurts opens; what opens admits light. Pain repurposed as entrance.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the wound. The line inverts injury into opportunity: sealed surfaces admit nothing, while breaks let light through. Healing completes the circuit the hurt began.
lessonContent:
Breakage can function as aperture.
Sealed surfaces admit nothing new.
Pain repurposed becomes entrance, not just injury.
Inversion turns affliction into instrument.
Share this: name one wound that later let light in.

title: The Drop Reversed
question: Feeling tiny, you call yourself a drop in a vast sea. Rumi reverses the image entirely. What does he say you wholly contain?
correctExplanation: The ocean — the drop contains the sea entire. Smallness inverted: consciousness holds the world it feels lost inside.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the ocean. Rumi flips scale inside out: you are not a fragment adrift but the whole, locally expressed. Containment runs both directions at once.
lessonContent:
Scale inversions dissolve smallness at a stroke.
Containers and contained trade places in mystic logic.
Feeling lost can signal unrecognized vastness.
Reverse every belittling image once to test it.
Share this: tell someone they hold an ocean today.

title: The Reed's Lament
question: Cut from its riverbed and hollowed into a flute, the reed sings of one absence above all. What does its music mourn?
correctExplanation: Separation — every note mourns the riverbed left behind. Music as homesickness: beauty powered by distance from source.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is separation. The flute's song is the sound of exile — sweetness proportioned to distance from origin. All longing, Rumi suggests, remembers an uncut wholeness.
lessonContent:
Music can be homesickness made audible.
Sweetness often proportions to distance from source.
Exile narratives explain universal longing.
Trace every lament back to its riverbed.
Share this: listen to one song as pure homesickness.

title: The Wise Trade
question: Rumi advises selling one prized possession of the mind and buying confusion with the proceeds. What should the seeker purchase?
correctExplanation: Bewilderment — trading cleverness for wonder. Certainty closes; confusion opens. The seeker profits by going bankrupt in answers.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is bewilderment. Cleverness defends the known; wonder explores the real. Rumi's economics: sell the fortress, buy the horizon.
lessonContent:
Certainty closes doors that wonder opens.
Confusion can be purchased deliberately.
Cleverness defends; bewilderment explores.
Bankruptcy in answers is wealth in questions.
Share this: trade one certainty for a question today.

title: The Clever Confession
question: 'Yesterday I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today I am wise, so I am changing… ' Whom does the wise one work on?
correctExplanation: Themselves — ambition matured from world-editing to self-editing. The only renovation project under full jurisdiction.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is themselves. Cleverness assigns homework to billions; wisdom assigns it to one. Jurisdiction decides the project: self is the sole editable territory.
lessonContent:
Jurisdiction decides every renovation project.
World-editing is cleverness avoiding homework.
One editable territory exists: the self.
Maturity redirects ambition inward.
Share this: assign yourself one renovation this week.

title: The Returning Loss
question: Rumi counsels against grieving what vanishes, promising it comes back transformed. What returns in another form?
correctExplanation: Anything lost — nothing exits, only re-enters differently. Grief misreads transformation as theft.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is anything lost. Loss is reframed as relocation: forms perish, essences recur. Mourning the shape misses the substance returning.
lessonContent:
Forms perish; essences recur in new shapes.
Grief can misread transformation as theft.
Return promises reframe every farewell.
Watch for comebacks wearing strange costumes.
Share this: trace one loss that returned transformed.

title: The Burned Barn
question: A farmer's barn burns to ash, and that night he finally sees the sky clearly. What becomes visible through the ruin?
correctExplanation: The moon — the roof that blocked the sky is gone. Loss as skylight: structures that sheltered also obscured.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the moon. The barn roof had hidden the heavens for years; fire removed the obstruction. Every shelter doubles as a blindfold — ruin occasionally restores the view.
lessonContent:
Shelters double as blindfolds over time.
Ruin occasionally restores obstructed views.
Roofs block heavens as well as rain.
Ask what each loss unblocks, not just what it burns.
Share this: name one ruin that restored a view.

title: The Grief Rhythm
question: When grief cracks you open, Rumi prescribes a surprising physical response rather than stillness. What should you do?
correctExplanation: Dance — movement metabolizes breakage. Stillness nurses cracks; rhythm weaves them into pattern.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is dance. Rumi's prescription moves grief through muscle instead of marinating in it. Broken-open is a doorway, and doorways are for passing through in motion.
lessonContent:
Movement metabolizes what stillness marinates.
Breakage can be danced through, not just endured.
Rhythm weaves cracks into pattern.
Prescriptions beat descriptions for grief.
Share this: move your body through one heaviness today.

title: The Divine Language
question: Words divide and doctrines quarrel, but Rumi names one wordless medium as the speech of the sacred itself. What is it?
correctExplanation: Silence — the one tongue no doctrine disputes. Where words fork into sects, quiet stays whole.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is silence. Every claim spoken splits listeners; the unsaid unites them. Rumi's linguistics: truth's native tongue needs no translation.
lessonContent:
Spoken claims split; the unsaid unites.
Translation needs vanish in wordlessness.
Doctrines quarrel where quiet agrees.
Practice one conversation held mostly in pauses.
Share this: share five minutes of silence with someone.

title: The Dark Elephant
question: Blindfolded men feel one beast in a dark room — one the trunk, one the leg — then quarrel over its shape. What does each man hold?
correctExplanation: One part mistaken for the whole — trunk-men versus leg-men, both right locally, both wrong globally. Perspective + certainty = quarrel.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is one part. Each gripped a genuine piece and universalized it. Rumi's epistemology: touch is honest, extrapolation is the liar. Wholeness needs pooled reports.
lessonContent:
Touch is honest; extrapolation lies fluently.
Local rightness plus global certainty equals quarrel.
Wholeness requires pooled, humble reports.
Ask which part of the elephant you are holding.
Share this: pool three views on one dispute today.

title: The Complaining Chickpea
question: A chickpea protests the boiling pot until the cook explains the heat's purpose. What does the boiling bestow?
correctExplanation: Flavor — suffering as seasoning. The pot that tortures raw chickpeas perfects them; heat with purpose is cuisine, not cruelty.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is flavor. The cook's defense reframes torment as preparation: unboiled stays hard and bland. Trials season what comfort leaves raw — maturation needs temperature.
lessonContent:
Heat with purpose is cuisine, not cruelty.
Trials season what comfort leaves raw.
Protest measures temperature, not meaning.
Ask the cook before condemning the pot.
Share this: reframe one hardship as seasoning aloud.

title: The Parrot's Lesson
question: A caged parrot learns that only the apparently dead are carried out past the bars. What must the seeker do before dying?
correctExplanation: Die before dying — shed the self while living, and no cage can hold what's left. Freedom through preemptive dissolution.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is die before dying. The parrot's ruse literalizes mystic practice: release identity first, and bars lose their prisoner. Cages confine selves, not the selfless.
lessonContent:
Cages confine selves, never the selfless.
Release identity and bars lose prisoners.
Ruses can literalize the deepest practices.
Freedom begins before any door opens.
Share this: shed one identity-label for a day.

title: The Worn Necklace
question: You ransack room after room hunting a diamond necklace, while it has hung around your throat the whole frantic search. Where was the treasure?
correctExplanation: The necklace — worn throughout the hunt. Seeking presumes absence; the treasure presumes presence. Stop searching rooms, feel your throat.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the necklace. The frantic rooms dramatize outward seeking; the throat holds the inward answer. Presence overlooked is the oldest treasure plot.
lessonContent:
Seeking can presume an absence that isn't.
Outward hunts miss inward holdings.
Feel the throat before ransacking rooms.
Presence overlooked is the oldest plot.
Share this: inventory one treasure already worn.

title: The Inward Knowing
question: Books can teach one kind of intelligence, but Rumi insists another flows up from inside like a spring. What knowing comes from within?
correctExplanation: Inner knowing — spring-water wisdom versus cistern-stored schooling. One is collected, the other erupts.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is inner knowing. Acquired intellect stocks cisterns; the soul's intelligence springs. Rumi's hydrology: dig within rather than hauling buckets from libraries.
lessonContent:
Springs outlast cisterns in dry seasons.
Collected knowledge differs from erupted wisdom.
Dig within before hauling library buckets.
Two intelligences need two kinds of schooling.
Share this: trust one spring-insight over a stored fact.

title: The Sorrow Compost
question: Grief feels like waste until Rumi hands you a gardener's task for it. What should sorrow be turned into?
correctExplanation: New growth — sorrow composted feeds what comes next. Waste is just fertility awaiting assignment.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is new growth. Gardeners never mourn manure; they assign it. Grief becomes topsoil for futures when worked rather than stored.
lessonContent:
Waste is fertility awaiting assignment.
Gardeners assign manure; mourners can assign grief.
Topsoil futures grow from worked sorrow.
Compost, don't warehouse, heavy feelings.
Share this: assign one grief a gardening task.

title: The Beyond Field
question: 'Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing there is a field.' What lies past all moral quarreling?
correctExplanation: A field — meeting ground past right and wrong. Morality's map ends; the meadow begins. Souls rendezvous beyond verdicts.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a field. Rumi plants reconciliation outside jurisdiction: no courts, no scorecards, just meeting. Beyond-quarrel space is a place, and arrival is a practice.
lessonContent:
Reconciliation needs ground outside jurisdiction.
Scorecards end where meadows begin.
Beyond-quarrel is a place, not an idea.
Arrival there is practice, not theory.
Share this: meet someone past one verdict today.

title: The Place Soul
question: 'Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place.' What should you become of every room you enter?
correctExplanation: Its soul — animating presence, not occupying furniture. Rooms have bodies (walls); visitors supply spirit.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is its soul. Standing somewhere is tenancy; ensouling it is stewardship. Rumi converts location into vocation: every place awaits its animating guest.
lessonContent:
Tenancy differs from stewardship entirely.
Places have bodies; visitors supply spirit.
Location converts to vocation on arrival.
Animate rooms instead of merely occupying them.
Share this: ensoul one room you enter today.

title: The Love Bridge
question: If love is a bridge, as Rumi says, what two shores does it join?
correctExplanation: Self and everything — the span from one to all. Bridges end isolation without erasing either shore.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is self and everything. The bridge image keeps both banks: selfhood stands, and all-ness stands, joined. Union without dissolution is the engineering marvel.
lessonContent:
Bridges join without erasing either shore.
Union can preserve what it connects.
Isolation ends where spanning begins.
Span outward without abandoning selfhood.
Share this: bridge yourself to one stranger today.

title: The Triple Rescue
question: Rumi's triple counsel: be a lamp, a lifeboat, or a ladder. Though different tools, they share one role toward others. What is it?
correctExplanation: A rescuer — lamp guides, lifeboat carries, ladder lifts. Three metaphors, one vocation: being useful to the stranded.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a rescuer. Lamps guide the lost, lifeboats carry the drowning, ladders lift the stuck — different tools, identical job description. Usefulness is the shared vocation.
lessonContent:
Different tools can share one vocation.
Guide, carry, lift — usefulness wears many shapes.
Metaphor trios triangulate a single duty.
Ask what unlike images have in common.
Share this: play one rescue role today.

title: The Night Moon
question: The moon never apologizes for darkness — it shines within it. What must brightness stop avoiding?
correctExplanation: Darkness — the moon's canvas, not its enemy. Brightness needs contrast; avoiding night dims the only stage.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is darkness. Moons don't lobby for daylight; they work the night shift gloriously. Contrast is the precondition of radiance, not its obstacle.
lessonContent:
Radiance needs contrast to register.
Canvases look like enemies until used.
Night shifts can outshine day jobs.
Stop avoiding the background you need.
Share this: shine deliberately in one dark place.

title: The Dark Candle
question: 'What hurts you, blesses you. Darkness is your…' What everyday light does Rumi call darkness repurposed?
correctExplanation: A candle — darkness converted to illumination. Hurt becomes blessing by the same alchemy: source and gift swap costumes.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a candle. The sentence completes by promotion: darkness, renamed, lights the room. Alchemy language turns affliction into equipment.
lessonContent:
Affliction converts to equipment by renaming.
Darkness lights rooms once promoted to candle.
Source and gift constantly swap costumes.
Complete bleak sentences with luminous nouns.
Share this: rename one darkness as a candle.

title: The Cultivated Ache
question: Seekers beg for water — answers, signs, arrivals. Rumi says stop asking for water and request the ache instead. What should you get?
correctExplanation: Thirst — the ache that summons water. Answers chase the thirsty; the satisfied are never sought. Wanting is the magnet, not the lack.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is thirst. Begging water skips the engine: thirst draws wells, teachers, and rains toward itself. Cultivate the ache and arrivals volunteer.
lessonContent:
Aches summon what satisfactions never attract.
Wanting is the magnet; having is the rest.
Arrivals volunteer toward genuine thirst.
Request engines, not outcomes.
Share this: sharpen one wanting instead of one having.

title: The Inner Wall
question: 'Your task is not to seek for love, but to seek and find all the barriers within yourself.' What must the seeker locate?
correctExplanation: Inner barriers — love already circulates; walls dam it personally. The task is demolition, not acquisition.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is inner barriers. Seeking love outward chases what already flows; the work is removing dams. Find the wall and the river handles the rest.
lessonContent:
Rivers need un-damming, not chasing.
Walls are personal; currents are universal.
Demolition outperforms acquisition in love.
Locate dams before digging new channels.
Share this: name one inner wall to dismantle.

title: The Already Lovers
question: Lovers imagine meeting someday, somewhere — but Rumi says the union predates the journey. Where are lovers already?
correctExplanation: In each other — union before reunion. The journey doesn't manufacture closeness; it discovers preinstalled belonging.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is in each other. Meeting scenes dramatize what already holds: belonging predates introduction. Travel reveals; it rarely creates.
lessonContent:
Belonging can predate introduction entirely.
Journeys discover more often than they manufacture.
Reunion implies a union already installed.
Seek recognition, not construction, in love.
Share this: recognize one preinstalled belonging today.
